subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Gibson's direct theory and Gregory's constructivist theory

questions.q: In psychology, what does 'sensation' refer to?
options: The information detected and received by our sensory receptors
The brain's interpretation of incoming information
The tendency to see things in a particular way
The storage of visual images in long-term memory
questions.explain: Sensation is the raw data picked up by sensory receptors, before the brain makes sense of it.

questions.q: How is 'perception' best defined?
options: The way the brain interprets and makes sense of sensory information
The physical detection of light by the retina
The reflex response of receptors to a stimulus
The loss of sensory information over time
questions.explain: Perception is the brain's active organisation and interpretation of the sensations it receives.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the difference between sensation and perception?
options: Sensation is receiving information; perception is interpreting it
Sensation is interpreting information; perception is receiving it
Sensation and perception are two words for the same process
Sensation happens only in the brain; perception only in the eye
questions.explain: The receptors sense the stimulus, then the brain perceives (interprets) it.

questions.q: What is a defining feature of a monocular depth cue?
options: It can be used with only one eye
It requires both eyes working together
It only works in complete darkness
It depends on the eyes turning inward
questions.explain: Monocular cues, such as relative size and linear perspective, provide depth information using just one eye.

questions.q: Why are convergence and retinal disparity classed as binocular depth cues?
options: They both rely on using two eyes together to judge distance
They both work equally well with one eye closed
They both involve interpreting texture on a surface
They are both based on the height of objects in the visual field
questions.explain: Convergence (eyes turning inward) and retinal disparity (differences between the two retinal images) both require two eyes.

questions.q: The monocular cue of occlusion (superimposition) tells us that an object is nearer when it...
options: Partially blocks another object from view
Is higher up in the visual field
Appears smaller than surrounding objects
Has a smoother, less detailed surface
questions.explain: If one object overlaps and hides part of another, the overlapping object is perceived as closer.

questions.q: Which description matches the monocular cue of linear perspective?
options: Parallel lines appear to converge as they recede into the distance
Objects lower in the visual field are seen as further away
Nearer surfaces appear coarser and more detailed
The closer an object, the more the eyes turn inward
questions.explain: Linear perspective is the apparent meeting of parallel lines (such as railway tracks) at a distant point.

questions.q: How does the monocular cue of texture gradient indicate depth?
options: Surfaces look more detailed when near and smoother when far away
Objects appear brighter the closer they are
Distant objects are always positioned lower in the scene
Nearer objects cast longer shadows than distant ones
questions.explain: As a textured surface recedes, its detail becomes finer and less distinct, signalling greater distance.

questions.q: Standing on a straight railway line, Sam notices the two rails appear to meet in the distance. Which depth cue is Sam using?
options: Linear perspective
Retinal disparity
Colour constancy
Convergence
questions.explain: Rails are parallel but appear to converge with distance, which is the monocular cue of linear perspective.

questions.q: What is meant by 'size constancy'?
options: We perceive an object as staying the same size despite changes in its retinal image
We always see objects as smaller than they really are
Objects change colour as the light changes
Distant objects are perceived as larger than near ones
questions.explain: Size constancy keeps an object's perceived size stable even though its image on the retina shrinks with distance.

questions.q: As a door swings open, the image it casts on Priya's retina changes from a rectangle to a slanted shape, yet she still sees it as a rectangular door. Which constancy explains this?
options: Shape constancy
Size constancy
Retinal disparity
Motion parallax
questions.explain: Shape constancy allows us to perceive an object's true shape even when the retinal image is distorted by angle.

questions.q: Gibson's direct theory of perception is best described as which of the following?
options: A bottom-up theory where perception comes directly from environmental information
A top-down theory relying on stored knowledge and inference
A theory that perception is entirely learned through experience
A theory that all perception is based on visual illusions
questions.explain: Gibson argued perception is direct and bottom-up, driven by the rich information available in the environment.

questions.q: Gregory's constructivist theory argues that perception is...
options: An indirect, top-down process that uses prior knowledge and expectation
A direct process needing no prior experience
Completely innate and present from birth
Based only on the raw retinal image with no interpretation
questions.explain: Gregory saw perception as constructed indirectly (top-down) using past experience to interpret incomplete data.

questions.q: In Gibson's theory, what is meant by an 'affordance'?
options: The action possibilities that an object or surface offers a viewer
A mistaken hypothesis that causes an illusion
The tendency to expect a particular stimulus
The difference between the two retinal images
questions.explain: Affordances are the potential uses or actions an environment directly offers, such as a chair 'affording' sitting.

questions.q: How does Gregory's constructivist theory explain visual illusions?
options: They occur when the brain makes an incorrect hypothesis about the stimulus
They prove perception is entirely direct and error-free
They show that sensory receptors are faulty
They demonstrate that perception is fully innate
questions.explain: For Gregory, illusions arise when our knowledge-based hypotheses about a scene turn out to be wrong.

questions.q: A researcher claims that a moving observer receives all the information needed to perceive the world directly, without inference. Whose theory does this match?
options: Gibson's direct theory
Gregory's constructivist theory
Bruner and Minturn's theory
Gilchrist and Nesberg's theory
questions.explain: Emphasis on direct information from a moving observer with no need for inference is central to Gibson.

questions.q: What is a 'perceptual set'?
options: A tendency to perceive things in a certain way based on expectations and experience
The number of sensory receptors in the eye
A set of binocular depth cues used together
The complete loss of perception after brain damage
questions.explain: Perceptual set is a bias or readiness to notice and interpret stimuli in a particular way.

questions.q: Which of the following is a factor that affects perceptual set according to the AQA specification?
options: Motivation
Retinal disparity
Texture gradient
Convergence
questions.explain: The specified factors affecting perceptual set are culture, motivation, emotion and expectation.

questions.q: What did Bruner and Minturn's (1955) study of perceptual set demonstrate?
options: Expectation influenced whether an ambiguous figure was seen as a letter or a number
Hungry people perceived food pictures as brighter
Culture changed how depth cues were interpreted
Emotion made frightening images appear larger
questions.explain: The same ambiguous figure was read as 'B' among letters and '13' among numbers, showing expectation shapes perception.

questions.q: Participants who had gone without food judged pictures of food as brighter and more appealing. Which factor affecting perceptual set does this illustrate, as shown by Gilchrist and Nesberg?
options: Motivation
Culture
Expectation
Occlusion
questions.explain: Gilchrist and Nesberg (1952) found hunger (a motivational state) altered how food images were perceived.
